body.heading: The game
paragraphs: A game show offers you three doors. Behind one is a car; behind the other two are goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to reveal a goat, and offers you the chance to switch to door 2. Most people feel the two remaining doors must be fifty-fifty. They are not. Switching wins two times out of three.

When this puzzle was published in a magazine in 1990, thousands of readers - including professional mathematicians - wrote in to insist the answer was wrong. It is a wonderful reminder that probability can be certain and still feel impossible.

body.heading: Where the missing third goes
paragraphs: When you first picked door 1, you had a 1 in 3 chance of choosing the car, and a 2 in 3 chance of choosing a goat. That 2 in 3 does not vanish when the host opens a door. The host can always reveal a goat, and never reveals the car, so his choice quietly concentrates all of that 2 in 3 onto the one door he leaves closed for you.

If the 50-50 feeling still nags, scale the puzzle up. Imagine 100 doors: you pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors, leaving one other closed. Your first pick is still just 1 in 100. The surviving door carries the other 99 in 100. Switching now feels obviously right - and it is the same logic with three doors.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Play it at home with three cups and a coin hidden under one. Have a partner play the host, always revealing an empty cup after your first pick. Play 30 rounds always staying, then 30 rounds always switching, and tally the wins.
The switch column should pull clearly ahead. Small samples wobble, so if your first experiment is close, run it again - the two-to-one pattern is patient and will show itself.

takeaway: Switching wins two times out of three, because your first pick was probably wrong and the host's reveal quietly hands you the other doors' chances combined.
